comments.author: @arturasandriusaitis8832
comments.text:
Vilniaus Pilies kalno šiaurinėje papėdėje žmonių gyventa jau IV-III tūkstantmetyje prieš Kristų. Vėliau, pakilus Neries lygiui, gyvenvietė užlieta, o klimatui pasausėjus ir vandeniui nuslūgus, jos vietoje susidarė 0,2-1,3 m storio durpių sluoksnis. Pilies kalno papėdėje nuolatinė baltų gyvenvietė vėl atsirado I-jame tūkstantmetyje prieš Kristų. Jau I-ojo tūkstantmečio viduryje ant Pilies kalno stovėjo medinė pilis. IX-XI a. susiformavo Vilniaus protomiestas, XIII amžiuje aplink Pilies kalną ir ant jo jau plytėjo medinis lietuvių miestas. Karalių Traidenio (1269-1281 m.), Daumanto (1282-1285 m.), Butigeidžio (1285-1291 m.), Butvydo (1291-1295 m.) ir Vytenio (1295-1315 m.) laikais Pilies kalno vakarinėje papėdėje ant rago formos iškyšulio tarp senosios Vilnios upės vagos buvo pastatyta pirmoji Lietuvoje mūrinė pilis. Tai buvo ikigotikinė romaninė pilis. XIII a. dabartinės Arkikatedros Bazilikos vietoje buvo pastatyta pirmoji mūrinė katedra. XIII a. antroje pusėje-XIV a. pradžioje iškasus dabartinę Vilnios vagą, Žemutinė pilis kartu su Aukštutine pilimi virto salos tipo pilimi tvirtove. Jau tada apie Vilnių galima kalbėti kaip apie Lietuvos Valstybės sostinę. Karalius Gediminas (1316-1341 m.) Vilnių padarė nuolatine valdovo rezidencija. Jis išplėtė ankstyvąją romaninę pilį, jos šiaurės vakarų pusėje buvusį apvalų bokštą perstatė į galingą aštuoniakampį keturių aukštų bokštą. Būtent čia buvo tikrasis Gedimino bokštas, jo pamatai yra išlikę po Valdovų rūmais.
Tokia buvo Vilniaus pradžia. Vilnius buvo nuo amžių lietuvių gyvenamos jų etninės teritorijos beveik centre (šiek tiek į rytus). Lietuvių ir slavų etninė riba buvo toli rytuose, prie Minsko.

comments.text:
Vilnius was the capital of the huge Lithuanian empire - the Kingdom of Lithuania, later the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. As a result, it has one of the largest old towns in Europe (second only to Rome, apparently). After the Union of Lublin (1569), it was the largest city in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Polish cities were villages compared to it. After the occupation of 1795, Vilnius was the third largest city in all of ruzzian-controlled territory.

Vilnius - 60,000 inhabitants (1766)
Danzig - 36,000 inhabitants (1793)
Krakow - 23,591 inhabitants (1791)
Lviv - 20,000 inhabitants (18th century)
Poznan - 15,000 inhabitants (1772)
Torun - 10,000 inhabitants (18th century)
Elblag - 15,768 inhabitants (1781)
Warsaw - 14,000 inhabitants (1754)

replies.author: @RobertProksa-y5d
replies.text: The fact that Vilnius was not some grand metropolis is obvious to the naked eye when you compare what has survived to our day or been reconstructed in city centers. After all, the city center—the quality and monumental of its architecture—was and remains the true indicator of what a city actually is. Compared to the old centers of Gdansk, Krakow, Torun, Poznan or Lviv, the Vilnius market square and its adjacent quarters look very provincial and modest, if not to say poor, even though they are actually younger. It simply so happened due to a combination of circumstances that more of the old architecture survived in Vilnius than elsewhere. In places like Paris or Kraków, entire old quarters were actually demolished in the 19th century, whereas those in Vilnius remained because they were relatively new (after all, most of this architecture is not Gothic or Renaissance, but Baroque—several eras later). Yet, based on such a naive argument, you started building absurd theses. As for being a 'village,' Lithuania was effectively a village compared to Poland both in the distant past and today. You suffer from a similar delusion to the Russians: you think that if something looks huge on a map, it must be just as grand in reality. Meanwhile, that is simply not how it works."

replies.author: @RobertProksa-y5d
replies.text: Budy, do not fantasize. Neither was Lithuania a  empire, nor was Vilnius the largest city of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth ( PLC). Grand Duchy of Lithuania ( GDL) was a sparsely populated, poorly urbanized, and civilizationally and economically underdeveloped country. At the time the Union of Lublin was formed, Vilnius was only the 3rd or 4th city of the Union, on par with Lviv, lagging far behind Gdansk and Krakow. At that moment, only two GDL cities made it into the top 10 cities of the Commonwealth—Vilnius ( 3-4) and Kaunas (9). The third largest city of the GDL ( Kiev) did not even rank in the top 10. This was the reality of the GDL's actual potential. As a side note, in the 18th century leading up to the partitions, the PLC  lost about 30% of its population due to wars, epidemics, and the resulting famine. This loss primarily affected the urban population, where the rate even exceeded 50%. Therefore, using dates from this period is pure manipulation aimed at proving a specific thesis. It is enough to recall that while Warsaw's population surpassed 100,000 by 1792 ( so it was the largest city in the PLC at the time of the state's liquidation), this number dropped to 60,000 by 1800 as a result of the partitions, only to exceed 140,000 in 1829. It is also worth mentioning that in 1720, Vilnius had only about 4,000 inhabitants. So, as you can see, by applying your methodology (cherry-picking dates that suit me), I could easily prove the exact opposite. In reality, the rapid development of Vilnius occurred in the second half of the 18th century. Until then, it was a relatively poor, medium-sized city with provincial architecture. Thus, it is hard to call it a truly old city. In this sense, it resembles Saint Petersburg, albeit on a provincial scale when it comes to the quality of the architecture. In Vilnius, it is difficult to find monumental buildings (the indicator of a city's power) predating the mid-18th century. Therefore, by European standards, the Old Town of Vilnius is not that old at all, meaning it is not that valuable.
